title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem and CRT Lattice Connections
description: Dirichlet's approximation theorem (1842): for any real α and N ≥ 1, there exist p, q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N and |qα - p| < 1/N. Proved via pigeonhole principle on fractional part binning. Includes mediant/Stern-Brocot property, lattice point theorem, golden ratio identities, and CRT non-coprime solvability examples connecting Diophantine approximation to lattice geometry.

overview.historicalContext:
Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet (1805-1859) proved this theorem in 1842, establishing the foundation of Diophantine approximation. The result shows that every real number can be well-approximated by rationals, with quality inversely proportional to the denominator. The proof introduced the 'pigeonhole principle' (Schubfachprinzip) to number theory.

The theorem was later refined by Hurwitz (1891), who showed the optimal constant is 1/√5, achieved by the golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2. The connection to the Chinese Remainder Theorem arises through lattice geometry: CRT solvability corresponds to lattice coset membership, and Dirichlet-style counting arguments on lattice points yield approximation results.

The Stern-Brocot tree (Stern 1858, Brocot 1861) provides the algorithmic structure for generating best rational approximations, with the mediant operation as its fundamental building block. This connects to continued fractions, which give the sequence of best approximations to any real number.
overview.problemStatement:
**Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem**: For any real number α and any positive integer N, there exist integers p and q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N such that |qα - p| < 1/N.

Equivalently: |α - p/q| < 1/(qN) ≤ 1/q².

This is proved via the pigeonhole principle: N+1 fractional parts {0·α}, {1·α}, ..., {N·α} mapped to N bins of width 1/N in [0,1). Two must share a bin, giving a good approximation.
overview.text: Dirichlet's approximation theorem via pigeonhole principle, with connections to CRT lattice theory, Stern-Brocot mediants, and the golden ratio as the worst-case approximation target.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Dirichlet's theorem** is proved by defining a bin function binFn : Fin(N+1) → Fin(N) that maps each index i to the bin ⌊N · fract(iα)⌋. By Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt (pigeonhole), two indices share a bin. Their fractional parts are within 1/N, and the difference gives the desired approximation.

The **mediant theorem** uses cross-multiplication: a/b < c/d implies a·d < c·b, and the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) satisfies both a(b+d) < (a+c)b and (a+c)d < c(b+d).

The **golden ratio** identities follow from √5² = 5 and algebraic manipulation with nlinarith.
keyInsights: **Pigeonhole on fractional parts**: The N+1 values {kα} for k = 0,...,N lie in [0,1). Binning into N intervals of width 1/N guarantees a collision, which yields the approximation. The proof is entirely constructive once the collision is found.

**Cast gymnastics**: The main technical challenge is managing coercions between ℕ, ℤ, and ℝ. Natural subtraction (j - i where j > i as ℕ) must be cast to real subtraction (↑j - ↑i) via Nat.cast_sub, and integer floor differences must be split via Int.cast_sub.

**Golden ratio optimality**: φ = (1+√5)/2 is the hardest-to-approximate irrational because its continued fraction [1;1,1,...] has the slowest convergence. Hurwitz's theorem says 1/√5 is the best universal constant for |x - p/q| < C/q².

**CRT-lattice duality**: Non-coprime CRT solvability (gcd(m₁,m₂) | (a₁-a₂)) is equivalent to a lattice point existing in a shifted sublattice. This geometric viewpoint unifies Dirichlet-style counting with modular arithmetic.

**Stern-Brocot mediant**: The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) of a/b and c/d always lies strictly between them. This operation generates all rationals in lowest terms and produces best approximations via binary search.

sections.title: Pigeonhole Setup for Fractional Part Binning

conclusion.summary: We have formalized Dirichlet's approximation theorem via the pigeonhole principle, establishing the foundational result of Diophantine approximation. The proof demonstrates how finite combinatorics (pigeonhole on N+1 fractional parts) yields a powerful analytic result (rational approximation quality 1/(qN)). The connections to CRT lattice structure, Stern-Brocot mediants, and the golden ratio show how number theory, combinatorics, and geometry interweave in the theory of Diophantine approximation.
implications: Every irrational has infinitely many rational approximations p/q with quality better than 1/q²
The golden ratio is the hardest-to-approximate irrational (Hurwitz constant √5)
CRT solvability for non-coprime moduli reduces to lattice point counting
Dirichlet's method extends to simultaneous approximation in higher dimensions (Minkowski's theorem)
